n: A new set of instructions begins. Coming right after the failure at Kadesh in chapter 14, these laws quietly promise that Israel will still reach the land, even though that generation will not.

f.g: spake = spoke

n: The Lord speaks of “when,” not “if.” Despite the people’s rebellion, His promise of a homeland stands, and the next generation will offer these sacrifices there.

f.g: The land where they will settle and live — Canaan.

n: These rules apply to voluntary and festival offerings of cattle or sheep. “Sweet savour” pictures God being pleased with sincere worship, as a pleasant smell rising from the altar.

f.g: A gift given simply out of a willing heart, not because it was required.

n: Every animal sacrifice was to be joined by a grain offering of flour and oil. Bread, oil, and life together acknowledged that all of Israel’s food came from God.

f.g: In KJV English “meat” means food in general; this is a grain (flour) offering.
A tenth of an ephah — roughly two to four pounds of flour.
A liquid measure, perhaps about a gallon (scholars’ estimates vary).

n: Wine was also poured out as a drink offering with each lamb. A small, joyful touch: the produce of vineyards Israel did not yet own is already part of the plan.

f.g: Wine poured out beside the altar as a gift to God.

n: A larger animal called for a larger grain offering. The amounts grow with the size of the sacrifice, keeping the whole offering in proportion.

f.g: An adult male sheep.

n: With a ram, the wine offering also increases to a third of a hin. The detail shows that worship was meant to be orderly and complete.
Now the rules turn to the largest offering, a young bull, whether given as a burnt offering, to fulfill a vow, or as a peace offering shared in fellowship.

f.g: A young bull.

n: A bull required three tenths of flour mixed with half a hin of oil — the biggest grain offering of the set.
Half a hin of wine accompanied the bull. Together the animal, grain, oil, and wine formed one complete gift that pleased the Lord.
This verse sums up the scale: bull, ram, lamb, or young goat, each had its matching portions.

f.g: A young goat.

n: If a person brought several animals, each one needed its own grain and drink offering. Nothing was to be done halfway.
Native-born Israelites were to follow this pattern every time they offered a sacrifice by fire.

f.g: Native-born Israelites.

n: Foreigners living among Israel who wished to worship the Lord were welcome to do so, following the same pattern as everyone else.

f.g: A resident foreigner — someone not born an Israelite but living in their community.

n: A striking principle of equality: before the Lord the outsider and the Israelite stand alike. God’s covenant has always reached beyond one family line.

f.w: as ye are, so shall the stranger be

n: One law for all. The repetition stresses that God does not keep two standards, one for insiders and one for newcomers.
A second set of instructions begins, again looking ahead to life in the promised land.
Again the Lord speaks confidently: He is the one bringing Israel into the land.

f.g: whither = to where

n: When Israel first eats the bread grown in Canaan, they are to set some apart for the Lord. The first portion belongs to the Giver.

f.g: A portion “lifted up” or set apart from the rest and given to the Lord (and His priests).

n: A cake from the first batch of dough is given to the Lord, just as the first grain from the threshing floor was. It is a way of saying “thank you” before eating.

f.g: A flat, hard place where harvested grain was beaten to separate the kernels from the husks.

n: This is to be a lasting practice. Giving God the first, rather than the leftovers, teaches gratitude in everyday life.
Now the Lord addresses failure. What happens when Israel unintentionally falls short of His commandments?

f.g: Gone astray or made a mistake without meaning to.

n: This covers any of the commandments given through Moses, from the beginning onward. God expected that His people would sometimes slip.
If the whole community sins without realizing it, they offer a bull as a burnt offering and a goat as a sin offering together. There is a remedy for collective mistakes.

f.g: Here, sin done unintentionally or without knowing it.

n: Through the priest’s atonement the people are forgiven. These sacrifices pointed forward to Jesus Christ, whose Atonement truly covers sins committed in ignorance.
Forgiveness reaches the whole congregation — including the foreigners living among them.
An individual who sins unintentionally brings a year-old female goat as a sin offering.

f.w: she goat of the first year

n: The priest makes atonement and the person is forgiven. God does not leave honest mistakes unresolved; He provides a way back.
Again, the same merciful law applies to Israelite and stranger alike.
Deliberate, defiant sin is different. To sin “presumptuously” is to sin with a raised fist, knowing better. Such a person insults the Lord and is cut off from the people.

f.g: Hebrew “with a high hand” — openly, defiantly, on purpose.
reproacheth = insults, shows contempt for
Removed from the covenant community; sometimes this meant death.

n: The reason: such a person has despised God’s word itself. The guilt rests on them alone. The contrast teaches that God weighs our intentions, not just our acts.

f.w: despised the word of the LORD

n: A real example follows: a man was caught gathering firewood on the Sabbath. Coming right after the law on defiant sin, the story seems meant to illustrate it.
Those who found him brought him to Moses, Aaron, and the community, rather than taking matters into their own hands.
They held him in custody because the penalty had not yet been made clear. Moses waited for the Lord’s direction instead of guessing.

f.g: in ward = under guard, in custody

n: The Lord declared the death penalty. To modern readers this is very hard; in Israel’s setting the Sabbath was a sign of the covenant itself, and open defiance of it threatened the whole people’s bond with God.

f.g: Outside the camp, keeping the community’s holy space undefiled.

n: The sentence was carried out as the Lord commanded. The story shows how seriously the covenant of the Sabbath was taken at that time.
A gentler instruction closes the chapter, given as a lasting help to remember.
Israelites were to wear tassels on the corners of their clothes, each with a blue cord. Blue was a costly, royal color, reminding them that they belonged to a holy King.

f.g: Tassels on the corners of a garment (Hebrew tsitsit), still worn by many Jews today.
ribband = ribbon; a blue (or violet) cord.

f.w: fringes in the borders of their garments

n: The tassels were a visual reminder: every glance would recall God’s commandments and help them resist following every desire of their hearts and eyes into spiritual unfaithfulness.

f.g: A strong biblical image for unfaithfulness to God, especially idolatry, compared to betraying a marriage.

n: The purpose of remembering is doing — and becoming holy. Latter-day Saints may think of the sacrament prayers, where we promise to “always remember him.”
The chapter closes with God’s signature: “I am the LORD your God,” who freed them from Egypt. Every law rests on that relationship and that rescue.

f.g: Small capitals render the divine name YHWH (Jehovah), whom Latter-day Saints understand to be the premortal Jesus Christ.
